title: Akshardham Arts & Cultural Center dedicated to BAPS in Robbinsville, Central New Jersey Just…
text:
Akshardham Arts & Cultural Center dedicated to BAPS in Robbinsville, Central New Jersey 

Just visited this campus today and it was truly impressive in its scope and ambitious architecture! This is the latest and grandest sprawling campus in the US built on 185 acres, 200 ft spires (cost $100M), dedicated to a Hindu denomination or a faith tradition to a lineage of gurus.   

The facility, only recently dedicated with parts still under construction with additional buildings, is easily accessible off route 295 in Mercer county, has ample parking, is free and welcomes all. The consumer experience is outstanding with state-of-art techy facilities, volunteer staff, no wait despite a full parking lot, a dedicated smartphone app, low level music, etc. There is a disney-esque quality to the actual experience and will undoubtedly be a destination for anyone, much like the famous cathedrals regardless of your faith!  A visit evokes serenity, solemnity, a contemplative state and calm in an otherwise harried world. Expect to devote 2-3 hours for an immersive visit.  At this early juncture, what was not present are cultural or educational programs or interactive displays, which are no doubt part of the additional buildings and a future plan?

The focus of the campus is on the intricate architecture, made of limestone and marble, with intricate hand-carving by traditional artisans in india and assembled on site. 
There is an exterior plaza with a dramatic 49 foot bronze statue of the guru as a young boy as well as a large stepped pond symbolic merging of the 4 sacred rivers. Then you can proceed to the interior to a massive welcome center, in the style of a 17th century Haveli with pillars carved out of teak wood with skylights. The center has multiple smaller auditoriums showing a short film history, and on one end is a full cafe and a gift shop. A large hall on the other end leads to a massive outdoor courtyard bounded by 2 additional pools, multiple statues, a colonnade, and of course the imposing marble Akshardham (meaning an eternal abode of divine) in the distance. The exterior is intricately carved with images of elephants, village scenes, nature and there are murals in English quoting "values" from the vedas. There is a side entry with an area for shoe removal, then ascension to the second floor via a staircase (there is an elevator as the entire campus is fully accessible). The entirety of the mandir with columns, mandapams, stone pillars, domes are full of carved depictions of hindu tales, various murals, musical instruments, elephants. In addition, there are prominent figures of the six generations of BAPS gurus in various states of discourse. There are smaller depictions of Radha & Krishna and Vishnu. 

Faith is ultimately very personal and varied as to how it is practiced. This denomination appears to emphasize the lineage of gurus as a secular incarnation of god, with a personal relationship with the devotee in a teacher- student dynamic.  The focus is on the guru throughout, as this facility is devoted to BAPS and not formally a house of worship (i.e. no poojas, priests, slokas, offerings). There is much lesser emphasis on the traditional all-powerful deities (i.e. Brahma, Siva, Vishnu) or on rituals found in many temples. Though the roots remain steeped in the ancient Indian and hindu spiritual tradition and vedas, the historical faith has been “modernized” to appeal to a broader audience. In addition, there appears to be an appeal to unify and be inclusive and make the ancient tradition more approachable?
Ultimately, the visit evoked grandeur of scale and an awe of architectural achievement; but not necessarily a personal nostalgia that I directly connected with or with rapture. Is this just another face of hinduism to complement all others or will it be “ascendant” remains a question to consider.

Overall, I would highly recommend a visit to marvel at this campus that is in an unlikely location!  I would expect future offerings full of artistic and educational programs.

title: This article discusses an approach taken by Reno, NV with early success (to address homelessness…
text: This article discusses an approach taken by Reno, NV with early success (to address homelessness in about 600 adults). Productivity in the construction sector (which represents 4% US GDP) has fallen by 40% (per worker since 1970); this is opposite of what has happened in all other industries. When productivity falls, prices rise! US is 4M housing units short of where we ought to be.  Reasons are multifactorial but constructing from scratch on site is a major factor as well as the many small independent local firms limits efficiencies of scale. Alternative models of "pre-fab" modular construction are clearly the direction for the future as it will substantially lower costs (i.e. most of the manufacturing will be on a factory floor, and actual "assembly" on site will require much lower skill so more people will enter the industry so labor costs go down).  We need a groundswell of support (i.e. political will) to facilitate this trend (where modular is currently only 6% in US, whereas it is 15% in Japan and 80% in Sweden)! In fact, this modular building concept has been used in building 50 story towers as well. These issues were discussed in a brilliant podcast on Freakonomics.com, episode 566).

title: Just read David Brooks' "How to Know a Person," and I will attempt a brief review (mostly to…
text:
Just read David Brooks' "How to Know a Person," and I will attempt a brief review (mostly to memorialize my thoughts, perhaps others might find value). David is of course a noted columnist for the NYT who has a "conservative" world view on politics. He has been on a personal journey to become a humanist, as he detailed in an earlier book (The Second Mountain) and even more publicly in this one! His journey has resonated with me (more than his politics?). This book is based on his research tapping into noted authors, many interviews with psychologists. The book borders between being "therapy" and a self-help guidance to be a better conversationalist, to be more empathic, to be better at responding to trials and tribulations in others.  The book has some practical information with multiple lists for asking the right questions, the Big 5 personality traits, practices to develop empathy, discussion of "life tasks" to work through or accomplish, to become an "illuminator" rather than a "diminisher" or a "topper." David quotes widely from history and literature and offers many individual stories that makes the book quite educational and fun.  I found chapter 10 (friend who is in despair) to be a good discussion of depression; the section on "life tasks" to be a thoughtful exposition of stages of life most of us complete with varied success; or the chapter on the 5 personality traits.
There were sections that were quite preachy with a darker world view, somehow things are much worse now than in years past. For example, under the section "epidemic of blindness", he discusses "moral formation" and abandonment in American institutions since WW-2, sounding much like the MAGA-movement for the wistful good old days ("can't stay away from them politics"!). Some of us may prefer the America of today than the 1930s-40s-50s for many reasons (was an era pre-medicare, SS, civil rights, etc). Every use of the word "morality" in the book made me recoil!
In summary, I do recommend this book as a strong read, as we are all on a journey to be better at being human, to support each other, at being better listeners, etc! There are many tangible tools offered.

title: Just read Walter Isaacson's biography on Elon Musk.
text:
Just read Walter Isaacson's biography on Elon Musk.  Isaacson is a brilliant biographer (I previously read books on Jen Doudna and Crisper/gene editing as well as one on Steve Jobs); as a biographer, he is not a "fanboy" nor a Musk hater, but paints Elon as a complex and polarizing figure, a transformative genius with major character flaws.  Musk, who is only 52, has humble origins in South Africa with an abusive father, comes to the US (via Canada), then transfers to Univ of Penn and subsequently ends up in Palo Alto to become a serial entrepreneur. 

At heart, he is a physics/math nerd, a video gamer, a steely risk taker with high functioning Asperger syndrome (low empathy, high IQ). He had outsized visions for humanity from early on (i.e. to go to Mars to preserve humanity, sustainable energy on earth, etc); an indomitable will to distort reality and make things happen. He was a control freak, didn't suffer fools, didn't care about others or their feelings per se. He thrived in high drama, adrenaline-junkie, etc  There were near-death experiences for all his corporate ventures.  

His first venture was Zip2 in the early 90s, a humble software (with map locations crossed with a business directory), then PayPal (bought by eBay). The subsequent and unlikely success of SpaceX (which created a reusable rocket to power astronauts to orbit as well as an orbiting satellite system Starlink to provide internet back on earth), then Tesla (largest maker of electric vehicles), and other ventures (SolarCity, Boring, Neuralink, Optimus). Of course, the infamous recent purchase of Twitter, the sewer of public human discourse. As distracting and obtuse as the purchase of twitter might be, access to massive datasets (500M tweets/day) together with Tesla video feeds from Autonomous cars could represent a rich “training” source for an improved AI platform (X.AI).  

The biography carefully dissects his personal life, his multiple wives, partners, and many children, extended family of cousins, etc. The book paints a picture of lack of impulse control, a desire to be in the limelight, to be in control, "rules don't apply to me", a god-complex.  The many houses, private jet travel, parties into the early morning hours, and work till you drop. The book also explores Musk's political transformation from being Obama-supporting liberal dude, to a libertarian to self-serving obsession with free speech (especially with Twitter) to embracing right wing conspiracy theories.  Sometimes blurring what is a joke, what is being a provocateur, to what is being hateful and abusive, to being of personal benefit!  Remember, the dude is only 52, is the richest man on the planet, he is touching and driving critical and transformative areas (space travel with contracts with NASA, car production (with innovative industrial design fabs, battery facilities, active attempts at full self-driving), de facto charging standard and network, energy, emerging AI competitor to ChatGPT). 

What is fascinating is that Musk has one foot in software/computers but the other foot on physical, industrial objects that moves matter!  In that way, he is of a different breed than many other tech titans!  I wouldn't want to be married or work for the dude or be his competitor!  This is a must read biography, consider it volume 1 only as the story is unfolding in front of our eyes!

title: The "New Right" is a loosely organizd movement (intellectual, cutural, and poitical) in America…
text:
The "New Right" is a loosely organizd movement (intellectual, cutural, and poitical) in America that is challenging the traditional "wistful" conservatism of Reagan era (i.e which stood for small gov't, low taxes, pro-business, etc).  There is incoherance, at least for me, as to what counter-balances the American Center and center-left. This podcast, discussion between David French (a conservative attorney, evangelical christian turned journalist) and Stephanie Slade (a libertarian scholar) was illuminating for me, to give context for what is happening on the right and the reasons for disarray.  This is not a "partisan discussion" but a more scholarly vocabulary lesson that might be useful to understand current and near term state of affairs.

title: Friends, here is a reliable and informative summary of the key issues for the public in Sept…
text:
Friends, here is a reliable and informative summary of the key issues for the public in Sept 2023 about the "updated covid vaccine"; basically it is being recommended for all adults (exceptions for allergy, etc). Interestingly, this is a monovalent vaccine (targets the optimal variant xbb.1.5 which also cross reacts with other variants in circulation). We have entered the era of an "annual covid shot" (not a booster per se) much like the annual fluvax that we are all used to in healthcare. There is NOTHING political about this vaccine, it is old fashioned gum-shoe epidemiology and science. For anyone trying to put a "political spin" on it, please don't!  
I have just gotten both the covid update and the annual fluvax. I am recommending it for my 88 y/o mother, other family, friends, and my patients. I urge all health care providers to review the attached and any other data that you wish (there is much out there, (see link to cdc) and to encourage the lay public, as there is intentional mis-information out there. I suppose an individual could elect to not get these vaccines (but not if you a healthcare worker); but they should not confuse the public and let the knowledgeable physicians and nurses make the case!  Disclosure: I am NOT being paid to write this, there is not a partisan agenda (fyi).  We all want a smooth, no drama covid cycle!

https://www.cdc.gov/respiratory-viruses/whats-new/covid-vaccine-recommendations-9-12-2023.html

title: Interesting dilemma for many stakeholders, including the consumer; what is clear is that oral…
text: Interesting dilemma for many stakeholders, including the consumer; what is clear is that oral phenylephrine doesn't work for reducing nasal congestion, unfortunately it is found in many popular OTC products. Inhaled is fine and there are many alternatives. The article addresses some nuances. Researchers have known this for decades, the special interests have been pushing back, but why the FDA is taking this position now is unclear. It will likely produce much confusion for the consumer, including litigation, etc.

text:
This is the biggest story that I have been trying to understand! title: Is it appropriate for a physician to highlight or discuss social policy issues?
text:
Is it appropriate for a physician to highlight or discuss social policy issues? Well, here I go: homelessness and attendent consequenses are complex but why is the idea of targeted cash transfers such a polarizing issue, when the data as to benefits are so consistently clear? The stereotype that such transfers will be used frivolously (i.e. to buy booze and drugs) and lead to life-long dependence and laziness is unsubstantiated by data. It is high time for us to take bias and emotion (and politics) out of this and make data-driven policy decisions. This is not "do good-ism" but driven by financial return! See the randomized controlled trial recently published in PNAS that is quite illustrative and compelling (among many other studies), with lessons and better practices (i.e. lump sum maybe better than monthly). Let's advocate for this.

A Canadian study gave $7,500 to homeless people. Here’s how they spent it.
The results show the power of cash transfers to reduce homelessness.

title: This is a powerful but simple concept of story-telling or "re-telling", where we are the…
text:
This is a powerful but simple concept of story-telling or "re-telling", where we are the protagonist or the hero of the story!  
The model is either an eagle-eye view versus a snake-eye view of our lives, often we’re just seeing what’s in front of us. I think that connecting with a myth or a story, whether it’s the Hero’s Journey or something else, can help us see the whole picture, especially when we’re feeling lost or stuck. Techniques involve reflective journaling, ask yourself who would star in the movie of your life, go on heroic adventures, be open to re-direction, and map out where you are on that journey.  Let's try it!

title: Just read the most eye-opening book by Bjorn Lomborg.
text:
Just read the most eye-opening book by Bjorn Lomborg.  He proposes that the poorer half of the world (low income and lower-middle income countries) can be dramatically benefitted by a series of 12 specific measures that are highly cost-effective with remarkable benefit within a short time.  He uses concepts of "benefit-cost-analysis" and "discounting" and identifies measures wherein $1 invested must return atleast $15 or more in benefits. The academic analysis indicates that in aggregate investing $35B annually between 2023 and 2030 will save 4.5M lives each year and generate $1.1 trillion in other benefit per year! The interventions can be broken down into medical/public health (i.e malaria, TB, maternal health, childhood immunizations, nutrition, chronic disease) and all other (i.e. education, agriculture R&D, e-procurement, skilled migration, and land tenure).  As to who should/could fund this (i.e. from local gov'ts, rich countries, or private philantropy).  Interestingly, he argues against certain interventions as not being cost-effective (i.e. climate policies, clean drinking water/sanitation, and peace-keeping forces)!  
The bottom-line: this is a sound analysis and is the blueprint we should follow, if we take emotion out of the picture and be ruthlessly efficient!

title: I came across an interesting topic (in the WSJ) about "synthetic alcohol"; lots of research…
text:
I came across an interesting topic (in the WSJ) about "synthetic alcohol"; lots of research going on to provide the 'happy effects" of drinking alcohol without the negative side effects (hangover or the addictive effects). It appears that GABA-specific agonists (i.e. Alcarelle, GABA Labs in late phase trials) might be the trick.  Another strategy is by Amygdala Neurosciences to target and block an enzyme critical in dopa pathways, reducing cravings. Indivior has a nasal spray as pre-treatment before a night out!  FGF21 is another strategy.  Bottomline:  many serious pursuits to pharmacologically "distill" happiness!  Will keep an eye on this sector as to where it will lead (no doubt there will be unintended consequences?).  

https://www.wsj.com/articles/synthetic-alcohol-no-hangover-511fc418
